articles.title: Carnegie Mellon is putting computer science courses on YouTube for free
articles.summary: Carnegie Mellon is putting computer science courses on YouTube for free

top_comments: Hi! I'm Phillip Compeau, I teach in Carnegie Mellon's Griffin School of Computer Science, and I run CS Learn, which launched today.We're releasing full semesters of lectures from current CMU computer science courses across a variety of topics, with one course premiering each day this week. More courses come in January.Yes, MIT got here 25 years ago :). What I'm excited about is how we're doing it: a few of our students built tools that automate a lot of the production work, so a small team can get a course out quickly and still have people review every lecture.We'll have lots more coming across a wide array of subjects. I'd love to know if there are topics you would like to see us cover!

To those asking why this is still valuable in the age of AI?If you learn the fundamentals properly, then AI will be a power tool for you. If you don’t, then it will replace you.I don’t mean this in an aggressive “you better get used to it” sense, I realize there’s nuance - but this is the version that fits on a T-shirt.
Very excited to see that 15-259 Probability and Computing will be available soon. That was one of my favorite classes at CMU during my undergrad.

articles.title: Rust changed me as a developer
articles.summary: Rust changed me as a developer

top_comments: A standard piece of advice is that every developer should do a major project in every big language family. A Lisp, an OO language, a functional language, Prolog, VHDL or Verilog, a Forth, et cetera. They'll all make you think differently and teach you lessons you will use outside of the family.

One of the things that I think makes Rust unique is that it acknowledges the possibility of human error. I think it’s also one of the most controversial too: there are certain people who get an ego hit at the insinuation that they ever could have written C code with mistakes.Instead of hoping you remember to check for NULL, Rust forces you to make a decision on how to handle the possibility of failure. Sure, you can still pick a bad decision (unwrap) but that is at least a specific decision and you can’t forget to do it.You can take it even further with things like the newtype pattern. If you have lots of numeric IDs (project ID, user ID, etc) you can give them distinct types so you don’t mix them up.So Rust taught me I can program defensively against my own brain, which sometimes gets tired or lazy or distracted.

> Any language without sum types now feels impoverished to me.I wholeheartedly agree. I learned this lesson from learning Haskell, before I was even aware of Rust and before Rust had its 1.0 release. One of the reasons I was first excited about Rust in fact was precisely that it had a type system like that of Haskell.
